title: Climate and the future
subtitle: Adapting the vineyard
objectives: Explain the effects of climate change on wine

steps.title: What's changing
steps.body: Harvests in many regions are two to three weeks earlier than in the 1980s. Alcohol has risen and acidity fallen. Extreme events, like frost after early budburst, hail, heatwaves, drought and wildfire, are more common. Smoke taint from fires affected California and Australia in 2020.

steps.title: Adapting
steps.body: Producers plant later-ripening grapes, higher or cooler sites, change canopy management for shade, and use drought-tolerant rootstocks. Regulations are changing too: in 2021, Bordeaux approved six new grapes, including Touriga Nacional, for trial in its AOCs. New regions like southern England, Tasmania and Denmark are rising.

steps.prompt: Which are adaptations to a warming climate?
steps.explanation: In heat, growers usually keep leaves to shade grapes, not remove them.

steps.title: Sustainability and packaging
steps.body: Glass bottles are the biggest part of wine's carbon footprint, often around 40%. Lighter bottles, bag-in-box, cans and paper bottles cut emissions. Shipping wine in bulk and bottling near the market also helps. Many producers now measure their footprint and seek certification.

steps.prompt: What is usually the largest part of wine's carbon footprint?
steps.explanation: Heavy glass bottles account for a large share of emissions, often around 40%.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Climate change brings earlier harvests and more extreme weather
Producers adapt with new grapes, sites and rules
Lighter packaging cuts wine's biggest footprint, glass
